title: New Zealand raises rates by consensus despite a split over inflation risks
summary: The September 2 meeting raised the OCR from 2.50% to 2.75% by consensus. All six members supported gradual removal of stimulus and the central projected rate path, but their assessment of the distributions around it differed. Four saw inflation risks tilted to the upside. Two judged them broadly balanced because downside risks to household demand could offset the danger of persistent pricing. The action reflected a shared preference for gradual adjustment, intended to reduce the risk that waiting would force a larger and more disruptive increase later (September decision and attributed meeting record).

The June-quarter CPI had by then been published. Annual inflation was 4.1%, driven largely by fuel and related costs. Excluding vehicle fuels, it was 2.9%. Most measures of core inflation lay within the 1–3% target band. Most measures of one- and two-year expectations had fallen since May and longer-term expectations remained near 2%. Expected wage growth was also consistent with a return to the midpoint. The Committee expected inflation to re-enter the target band by mid-2027 and reach 2% later that year. This timetable distinguishes a mechanical reduction in annual inflation once higher fuel prices drop out from the more demanding test of sustained convergence to the midpoint (meeting record, inflation assessment).

Growth appeared weak in the second quarter, with an uneven recovery beginning in the third. Export activity and investment were benefiting from foreign demand and export prices, particularly in the South Island and parts of the North Island. There had been limited spillover into other parts of the economy. Employment growth had not absorbed all new entrants to the labour market. Unemployment was particularly consequential in Auckland and Wellington, among young people and for the long-term unemployed. Some households moved toward regions with firmer labour markets. Higher saving, weak consumption and an incomplete translation of building consents into actual residential construction all cautioned against treating an export recovery as evidence of economy-wide tightness (meeting record, economic activity).

Domestic wholesale rates had already risen, lifting mortgage and business lending rates by comparable amounts. Exchange-rate appreciation also contributed to tighter financial conditions. Pass-through to term deposit rates was smaller, limiting the cost of new funding for banks. Members considered greater deposit-rate pass-through more consistent with the intended stance. A comparison of bank lending rates with the OCR may therefore capture only one side of transmission. The return to depositors, changes in bank funding spreads and effects on the incentive to save also deserve attention (meeting record, financial conditions).

Hayley Gourley, Karen Silk, Prasanna Gai and Anna Breman emphasized the possibility of persistent energy and petrochemical costs, front-loaded pricing and continued high administered-price inflation. Paul Conway and Carl Hansen also acknowledged the risk of firms embedding higher inflation but placed more weight on weak house prices and precautionary saving. Everyone regarded risks to growth as substantial, including that efficiency investment and technology could increase activity without a commensurate rise in employment. The decision offers a useful way to distinguish voting cohesion from economic consensus. A unanimous action was compatible with disagreement about which future development would warrant another increase and how quickly it might arrive (meeting record, named risk assessments and final decision).

questions.question: Was the labour market improving where central-bank stimulus was reaching demand?
questions.detail: Compare regional employment, participation, internal migration and spending with the strength of export receipts and local housing markets. Track actual construction after building consents rather than treating permits as completed investment. A recovery concentrated in export regions may leave considerably more spare capacity elsewhere than nationwide GDP implies.

questions.question: Were firms raising prices ahead of their own input-cost increases?
questions.detail: Measure timing and breadth of selling-price changes against actual imported fuel and petrochemical costs, controlling for contract intervals and inventory lags. Compare industries with small direct energy exposure. Front-loaded increases followed by persistent margins would be more consistent with the four members’ concerns than temporary price recovery after previously compressed margins.

questions.question: Did bank deposit pricing dilute the tightening reaching borrowers?
questions.detail: Match new term-deposit rates, mortgage and business loan rates with wholesale funding curves at the same maturity. Examine deposit flows, refinancing choices and bank funding spreads. If deposit rates rose much less than lending rates, the incentives facing savers and borrowers and the effect on bank margins would diverge.
